title: Sumerian City-States
capsule: The Sumerian city-states were a network of politically autonomous urban centers in southern Mesopotamia — including Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Nippur, Kish, and Umma — that developed from Neolithic agricultural villages into temple-centered polities between roughly 3400 and 2900 BC. Political power rotated among these centers, formalized in the Sumerian King List's concept of kingship 'descending from heaven' to successive cities; rivalry between Lagash and Umma over the Gu'edena border district produced some of the earliest recorded warfare, documented in the Stele of Vultures (c. 2450 BC). Sargon of Akkad unified the region by conquest around 2334 BC, transforming the independent city-state system into an imperial structure; Ur retained importance as the capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur (2112–2004 BC), after which Amorite invaders ended Sumerian political dominance.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The locations of individual city-states are confirmed by archaeology, but their territorial extents — fields, canals, satellite settlements — are reconstructed from cuneiform boundary documents and are subject to significant interpretive variation; the outer limits of influence shown at the dataset's scale are substantially conjectural.
